Mitochondria and cellular energy

Mitochondria are organelles found in most eukaryotic cells. They are often called the powerhouse of the cell because they produce the energy cells use to live and grow.

Inside each mitochondrion, cellular respiration breaks down fuel. The main product is ATP, a molecule that stores energy in a form other parts of the cell can spend. Mitochondria produce ATP continuously while oxygen is available.

The inner membrane holds the electron transport chain. As electrons move along that chain, protons are pumped outward and ATP synthase lets them flow back, producing ATP. This is the step that yields most of the cell's usable energy.

Cells with heavy energy demand, such as muscle cells, hold many mitochondria. The same process that produces ATP also releases carbon dioxide and water. Heat is a smaller byproduct in ordinary cells, and a larger one in brown fat.
